newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Reporters freed in Chechnya, others stay captive.
newsitem.headline: Reporters freed in Chechnya, others stay captive.

text.p: Four Russian journalists were released on Friday after three months of captivity in breakaway Chechnya and officials there said they hoped three more captives would be freed soon.
The four reporters looked pale as they arrived back in Moscow. President Boris Yeltsin said he welcomed their release and stressed Russia would not give in to terrorists.
"If anything happens, we never back down," Yeltsin, visiting Russia's second city of St Petersburg, told reporters. "Fighting terrorism is one of the main presidential programmes."

The journalists, Itar-Tass correspondent Nikolai Zagnoiko, and three reporters from Radio Russia, were seized in the breakaway Caucasus region two months before the signing of a peace deal between Yeltsin and Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov.
"We are really happy to be back. One cannot describe it in words," bearded, denim-clad Zagnoiko told Reuters.
A television crew from NTV commercial television is still being held, but Itar-Tass news agency quoted Chechen security chief Lecha Khultigov as saying the three would be freed soon.
He declined to give details of the operation which freed the other correspondents.

Kidnapping and other crimes are common in rebel Chechnya, where most men are still armed after the region's 21-month war with Russian troops and where jobs are scarce in an economy wrecked by the war.
Tens of thousands of people died in the fighting.

"I am happy today, but I am also sad because others remain hostages," said Tass director Vitaly Ignatenko. "I am sad because hostage-taking will continue...until it becomes calm in Chechnya, until their economy has been rebuilt."

The journalists and the officials meeting them at the airport said no ransom had been paid. "As far as we know, there was no ransom. Money would mean more hostages. They could have taken us hostage again in this case." Zagnoiko said.
"We did not pay anything, and Ignatenko did not pay a kopeck," said Nikolai Svanidze, chairman of Russian Television.
The freeing of the hostages, especially Russian journalists, has become a burning issue for Maskhadov who, surrounded by powerful field commanders, has yet to prove his grip on power.
Interfax new agency quoted Russia's Security Council Secretary Ivan Rybkin as praising Maskhadov's efforts.
"Maskhadov's success will bolster his influence among his voters," Rybkin said.
He said the freeing of the journalists would help develop the peace process in Chechnya. A Chechen delegation is in Moscow for talks on economic issues.

A Chechen police and commando raid last week freed six hostages, including an Austrian businessman. Maskhkadov, who has pledged to fight the wave of kidnapping, has said such operations would be staged often.
